cards.headline: Same rate move, different damage.
cards.body: Rates rise by the same amount for two bonds. A short one that repays next year barely flinches. A long one that repays in twenty years drops hard. The length of the loan decides how much a rate change hurts.

art.alt: Two planks pinned at one end under the same tip weight — a short one barely dips while a much longer one swings steeply down — the longer the bond, the harder a rate nudge moves it.

cards.headline: Duration measures the sensitivity.
cards.body: Duration is a single number for how much a bond's price reacts to interest rates. Roughly, it is the average number of years you wait for the bond's cash. Longer waits mean a bigger reaction — more duration, more risk.

cards.headline: The one-percent rule of thumb.
cards.body: Here is the handle: for each **1%** that rates rise, a bond's price falls by about its duration, in percent. Duration **7** means roughly a **7%** drop. Duration **3** means about **3%**. It runs the other way for rate falls.

cards.title: Longer duration, bigger fall
cards.caption: A one-point rate rise, three bonds. The longer the duration, the deeper the fall — a fifteen-year-ish bond loses roughly five times what a three-year one does.

cards.prompt: Rates jump one percent. Which bond's price falls more: a 2-year or a 20-year?
cards.explanation: The longer bond has far more duration — you wait two decades for your money, so its price is far more sensitive to rates. A one-point rise might cost it a good deal; it barely dents the two-year.

cards.headline: A close estimate, not a law.
cards.body: The duration rule is a first-order approximation. For a small rate move it is very accurate; for a large one it slightly overstates the fall, because the real price curve bends. It is the tool for intuition, not the last decimal.

cards.headline: The asterisk on 'safe'.
cards.body: A good-quality bond is safe from default — you will be repaid. It is not safe from rates. A long bond can lose real value the moment rates rise, even though every payment arrives on time. Two different risks, one asset.
